title: Impact of contour on aesthetic judgments and approach-avoidance decisions in architecture

findings.mechanism: curvilinear forms are experienced as softer and more pleasant
findings.quote: contour had a significant effect on beauty judgments, Z = −2.13, P < 0.05. Specifically, participants were more likely to judge spaces as beautiful if they had curvilinear than rectilinear contours (Fig. 2).
In contrast, contour had no effect on approach-avoidance decisions, Z = −1.27, P = 0.21 (Fig. 2).

findings.mechanism: pleasantness-the valence dimension of the affect circumplex-accounted for nearly 60% of the variance in beauty ratings.
findings.quote: pleasantness ratings (collected outside of the scanner) predicted beauty ratings (collected outside of the scanner), β = 0.73, P < 0.001 (Fig. 3).

findings.mechanism: pleasantness-the valence dimension of the affect circumplex
findings.quote: In fact, pleasantness ratings accounted for 58% of the observed variance in beauty ratings.
Pleasantness was once again a significant predictor of beauty judgment, β = −1.30, P < 0.001.
Pleasantness was a significant predictor of approach-avoidance decisions, β = −1.13, P < 0.001.
participants viewed spaces that they opted to "enter" for longer periods compared with spaces that they opted to “exit,” t(17) = 2.60, P < 0.05 (Fig. 4).
there was no difference in reaction time related to judging a space as “beautiful" or "not beautiful," t(17) = -0.84, P = 0.41.
contour had no effect on reaction time in the context of beauty judgments [t(17) = −0.72, P = 0.48]
or approach-avoidance decisions [t(17) = 1.29, P = 0.21].

findings.mechanism: ACC, a region strongly responsive to the reward properties and emotional salience of objects.
findings.quote: the contrast of curvilinear-rectilinear spaces revealed significant activation in ACC exclusively (Z = 3.54, x = −6, y = 42, z = −6, k = 11) (Fig. 5).

findings.mechanism: This specific prediction was derived from an earlier fMRI study in which it was shown that viewing rectilinear everyday objects activated the amygdala, suggesting that sharpness might serve as an early warning signal for potential danger (43).
findings.quote: The reverse contrast did not reveal any significant area of activation.

findings.antecedent: beauty judgment (beautiful/not beautiful) AND approach-avoidance decision (enter/exit)
findings.mechanism: to test Appleton's theory, we conducted a conjunction analysis... we examined whether judging a space as beautiful activates the same neural system as deciding to enter a space.
findings.quote: This conjunction analysis did not reveal any area of significant activation.

stimuli.description: 200 photographs of architectural spaces, half rectilinear and half curvilinear, balanced for ceiling height (high/low) and openness (open/closed).

tables.description: Brain regions showing significant activation (Z-score, cluster size) for parametric analyses of beauty ratings and pleasantness ratings.
key_stats: Z-scores for various brain regions, all p<0.001 (implied by Z-scores > 3.09 for cluster-corrected results)

limitations: Lack of amygdala activation for rectilinear-curvilinear contrast might be due to daily exposure to rectilinear spaces, leading to conditioning where sharp contours lose their threat signal value.
Longer exposure duration (3000 ms) might have triggered additional cognitive processing, depressing initial rapid amygdala response.
Amygdala's nonlinear response profile (maximal to extreme stimuli, less to average) might explain lack of activation if rectilinear stimuli were not 'extremely' threatening.
Built environments and landscapes might not be comparable in promoting evaluation for biological survival, suggesting context dependency.
Manipulating contour in landscapes might impact approach decisions and neural correlates differently than in built environments.
The study did not investigate how recruitment of specific brain structures differs between architects and laypeople, which is critical for understanding context in visual scene analysis.
